newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela tells South Africa's ANC to unite.
newsitem.headline: Mandela tells South Africa's ANC to unite.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela, on a mid-term swing through South Africa's nine provinces, has condemned personal rivalries in his ruling African National Congress (ANC).

Addressing supporters at closed meetings in Kimberley, capital of the sparsely populated Northern Cape province, on Saturday and Sunday, he insisted the party was bigger than the ambitions of its leaders.
"Let us put politics above personalities, programme above individualism...instead of embroiling ourselves in paralysing factionalism," he said in prepared remarks given to reporters.

Mandela's appeal came after a week of behind the scenes jockeying for a place in the queue to succeed him, either in December next year when he steps down as party president, or after his successor retires in 2009 at the latest.

"Healthy competition between individuals for election to posts is a natural part of any democratic organisation. But when personal competition starts to absorb all one's energies, when political programmes are forgotten and when solid grass-roots work is neglected, then matters become very serious," Mandela told one group.

Mandela, 78, referred only briefly in his prepared remarks to the dismissal earlier this month of the ANC government in Free State province and not at all to the race for the top party positions next year.
But sources said the two issues featured prominently in the ANC's assessment of their success halfway through the country's first five-year term of democratic government.
Free State Premier Patrick Lekota was forced by the ANC to quit following a bruising personality clash in what had been regarded as one of the party's most successful provincial administrations.

In a related development, Mandela was forced to deny allegations he had withdrawn support for Deputy President Thabo Mbeki as the ANC's next president and, by implication, the next president for up to 10 years from 1999.

Party sources said Mandela's reaffirmation in a closed meeting of the ANC's democratic right to elect its next leader in a secret ballot was deliberately misinterpreted by an Mbeki rival hoping to reopen the race.
